slots.practicalActivity: Sign up for (or log into) a real AWS Free Tier account, open the Management Console, and use the top services search to open S3, EC2, and CloudWatch one at a time without configuring anything -- the same three service families a DevOps engineer touches on day one for storing build artifacts, running workloads, and watching them.
slots.deliverable: A short note confirming you opened the AWS Console and located S3, EC2, and CloudWatch via services search, with one sentence on what each one would be used for in a deployment pipeline.

lessons.title: AWS Global Infrastructure: Regions & Availability Zones

slots.practicalActivity: In the AWS Console, use the Region selector in the top-right to switch between two real Regions (e.g. us-east-1 and eu-west-1) and watch EC2's resource list go empty each time -- resources don't follow you across Regions -- then open the account menu to find your 12-digit Account ID.
slots.deliverable: A written note naming the two Regions you switched between, what you observed about EC2's resource list in each, and your own AWS Account ID.

slots.practicalActivity: Take a self-guided tour of the Console's persistent chrome: the services search bar, the Region selector, the account/billing menu, and the CloudShell icon in the top nav -- open CloudShell and run aws --version from inside the browser with no local install.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot or note confirming AWS CloudShell opened in-browser and returned a real AWS CLI version string.

slots.practicalActivity: Open your account's Billing and Organizations pages (even on a single standalone account) to see where a real company's dev/staging/prod account split would live, and write one paragraph on why a DevOps team typically runs separate AWS accounts per environment instead of one shared account.
slots.deliverable: A written paragraph explaining why multi-account separation (dev/staging/prod) matters for a deployment pipeline, grounded in what you saw on the Organizations page.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a shared-responsibility table for EC2 specifically: what AWS manages (physical hardware, the hypervisor, facility security) versus what you as the deploying engineer manage (OS patching, security group rules, IAM access, what's running in the container or process on top).
slots.deliverable: A written shared-responsibility table for EC2 splitting AWS's responsibilities from a DevOps engineer's.

slots.practicalActivity: In the IAM console, create a real IAM user named devops-test-user (programmatic access only, no console password), create a group named DevOps-Engineers, attach the AWS-managed AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess policy to the group, and add the user to it; then create an IAM role trusted by the EC2 service to see the trust-policy screen roles use that users don't -- exactly the kind of role a deploy script running on an instance would assume.
slots.deliverable: A real IAM user inside a real IAM group with an attached managed policy, plus one IAM role created for EC2, both visible in the IAM console's Users, Groups, and Roles lists.

slots.practicalActivity: Walk the full EC2 launch wizard for a free-tier-eligible t2.micro/t3.micro instance (launching it, or stopping just before the final Launch click to avoid any charge) to see the AMI, instance type, security group, and attached EBS volume choices, then separately create a real S3 bucket and upload one small file -- the same bucket/object split a CI pipeline uses to stash build artifacts.
slots.deliverable: A real S3 bucket containing one uploaded file, plus a written note on the AMI, instance type, security group, and EBS volume size the EC2 launch wizard asked for.

slots.practicalActivity: In the VPC console, open your account's default VPC and inspect its CIDR block, its subnets (check each one's route table to tell public from private), and its default security group's inbound rules -- then edit that security group to open port 22 (SSH) only to your own current IP address, not 0.0.0.0/0.
slots.deliverable: A written note listing your default VPC's CIDR block, its public vs. private subnets, and a security group rule you edited to restrict SSH to your own IP.

slots.practicalActivity: Open AWS Pricing Calculator and build a real estimate for a small deployment stack (one EC2 instance running 24/7, one S3 bucket for artifacts, one small Lambda function for a deploy hook), then open Cost Explorer and AWS Budgets and create a real $5/month budget alert on your own account so a forgotten instance doesn't run up a bill.
slots.deliverable: A saved Pricing Calculator estimate for a 3-service deployment stack, plus a real $5 monthly budget alert configured in your AWS account's Budgets.

lessons.title: Users, Groups & Roles
lessons.chapterTitle: IAM Deep Dive for Data Engineers

slots.practicalActivity: Create a second IAM role, this time trusted by AWS Lambda instead of EC2, attach the AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess managed policy to it, and compare its trust-policy JSON (who can assume it) against the EC2 role's trust policy from the IAM Basics lab, identifying exactly what's different between the two.
slots.deliverable: A real Lambda IAM role with an attached policy, plus a written comparison of its trust-policy JSON against the earlier EC2 role's.

lessons.title: Policies & Permissions
lessons.chapterTitle: IAM Deep Dive for Data Engineers

slots.practicalActivity: Write a custom JSON policy granting only s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject on one specific bucket ARN (not *), attach it to devops-test-user, then use the IAM Policy Simulator to confirm an s3:DeleteObject call on that same bucket is correctly denied -- the exact scoping a CI/CD service account needs for an artifacts bucket.
slots.deliverable: A custom least-privilege JSON policy attached to a real IAM identity, plus a Policy Simulator result confirming s3:DeleteObject is denied while s3:GetObject/s3:PutObject are allowed.

lessons.title: Least Privilege for Data Pipelines
lessons.chapterTitle: IAM Deep Dive for Data Engineers

slots.practicalActivity: Rewrite your policy to scope it to one prefix inside the bucket (e.g. arn:aws:s3:::your-bucket/artifacts/*) instead of the whole bucket, following the lesson's ingestion-role pattern, then use CloudTrail's Event History to find and screenshot the real AccessDenied event your earlier s3:DeleteObject test generated.
slots.deliverable: A prefix-scoped IAM policy (not bucket-wide) verified in the Policy Simulator, plus a CloudTrail Event History screenshot showing the real AccessDenied call.

lessons.title: Cross-Service Access Patterns
lessons.chapterTitle: IAM Deep Dive for Data Engineers

slots.practicalActivity: Sketch in a doc a real cross-service access pattern a deployment pipeline needs: an EC2 instance role that can read one S3 artifacts prefix and write log lines to one CloudWatch Logs group, writing out the two specific resource ARNs it would need scoped access to, then create that role for real in IAM with both policies attached.
slots.deliverable: A real IAM role with two scoped policies attached (S3 read on one prefix, CloudWatch Logs write on one log group), plus the written design naming both resource ARNs.

slots.practicalActivity: Install the AWS CLI, run aws configure with a real access key pair for devops-test-user, then run aws s3 ls, create a test bucket with aws s3 mb, upload a small file with aws s3 cp, and set up a second named profile with aws configure --profile staging to practice switching between two identities the way a real engineer juggles dev vs. prod credentials.
slots.deliverable: A working AWS CLI configured with two named profiles against your own account, with terminal output showing a successful aws s3 ls under each profile.

slots.practicalActivity: Install boto3 (pip install boto3) and write a short Python script that creates an S3 client, lists your account's buckets, and uploads one local file to the bucket created in the previous slot -- the same kind of script a deploy automation step would run instead of shelling out to the CLI.
slots.deliverable: A working Python script using boto3 that lists your real S3 buckets and successfully uploads one file, with its console output captured.

slots.practicalActivity: Run the lesson's full round trip for real: aws s3 mb to create a uniquely named bucket, aws s3 cp to upload a text file, aws s3 ls and aws s3 cp <path> - to verify its contents from the terminal, then aws s3 rm followed by aws s3 rb to delete the object and the bucket, confirming cleanup so nothing keeps billing -- the verify-don't-assume habit that matters even more once deploys go through Infrastructure as Code.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output showing the full mb -> cp -> ls/verify -> rm -> rb round trip completed successfully against a real AWS account.

slots.practicalActivity: Open the official exam guides for AWS Certified Developer - Associate, SysOps Administrator - Associate, and DevOps Engineer - Professional, and write one paragraph mapping each exam's stated scope against this course's four chapters plus the Docker and Kubernetes courses ahead in this path, noting honestly which of the three is the closest-fit target once the path is further along.
slots.deliverable: A written mapping of the Developer Associate, SysOps Administrator Associate, and DevOps Engineer Professional exam guides against this course and the two containerization courses ahead, closing out the course.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can navigate the AWS Console and account structure, create and scope real IAM users, roles, and least-privilege policies, launch and inspect EC2/S3/VPC resources, and operate AWS from the CLI and SDK -- the account, identity, and tooling foundation the Docker and Kubernetes courses ahead in this path assume is already in place.
